title: Freedom: Negative, Positive and Republican
subtitle: Is a slave with a kind master free? Three answers to the oldest political question
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain Isaiah Berlin's distinction between negative and positive liberty and his warning about the latter
By the end you will be able to analyse freedom claims using MacCallum's triadic formula
By the end you will be able to state Pettit's republican ideal of freedom as non-domination and apply the 'kindly master' test
By the end you will be able to evaluate competing claims about whether markets enlarge or restrict freedom
hook:
Picture two people. The first is a slave in ancient Rome whose master happens to be gentle: he never beats her, rarely gives orders, and lets her spend her days as she pleases. The second is a free citizen of a modern democracy, crushed by a dozen regulations, paying taxes, stopping at red lights. Which of the two is more free?

If freedom simply means *not being interfered with*, the slave may win. She is interfered with less. Yet almost everyone feels that answer is absurd. She is not free at all; she lives at someone else's mercy, and could be sold tomorrow. Explaining exactly *why* she is unfree, and what that tells us about our own lives, is the task of this lesson. Along the way you will revisit Hobbes's account of liberty (Day 42), Rousseau's notorious claim that people can be forced to be free (Day 53), and Mill's harm principle (Day 62).

sections.heading: Berlin's Two Concepts
sections.body:
In 1958 the Oxford philosopher **Isaiah Berlin** (1909–1997) gave an inaugural lecture called *Two Concepts of Liberty*. Berlin had been born in Riga, witnessed the Russian Revolution as a boy in Petrograd, and emigrated to England. The shadow of Soviet communism and Nazism hangs over the lecture.

Berlin distinguished two questions.

**Negative liberty** answers: *What is the area within which a person is, or should be, left to do what they are able to do, without interference by others?* You are negatively free to the extent that no human being blocks your path. If the state forbids you to publish a pamphlet, your negative liberty shrinks. This is the liberty of Hobbes, who defined it as the absence of external impediments, and of Mill, who asked where the boundary of individual freedom should lie.

**Positive liberty** answers a different question: *What, or who, is the source of control that can determine someone to do this rather than that?* Positive liberty is **self-mastery**: being your own master, governing yourself according to your own reasons rather than being driven by external forces or by your own impulses. The addict who wants to quit but cannot is not interfered with by anyone, yet in the positive sense she is unfree.

Both ideas have deep roots. Negative liberty runs through the English liberal tradition. Positive liberty runs through Plato's rule of reason over appetite (Day 13), the Stoics (Days 25–26), Spinoza, Rousseau and Kant's ideal of autonomy (Day 56).

sections.heading: Berlin's Warning: The Divided Self
sections.body:
Berlin did not treat the two ideas as equally safe. His lecture is a warning about how positive liberty can be twisted.

The twist works in steps. Positive liberty says I am free when my *true* or *rational* self governs my *lower* self. But then someone may claim to know what my true self wants better than I do. Next, my true self is identified with something larger: the Nation, the Party, the Church, History. Finally, coercing me becomes, in theory, *liberating* me: forcing my empirical self to do what my real self 'really' wills. Berlin saw this logic behind Rousseau's line that whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be **forced to be free**, and behind twentieth-century tyrannies that imprisoned people in the name of their own emancipation.

Berlin's conclusion was **value pluralism**: human values are many, they genuinely conflict, and there is no single formula, no perfect society, in which all can be reconciled. Liberty may have to be traded against equality, security or justice. Recognising this, he thought, is a safeguard against utopian projects that sacrifice real people for an imagined harmony. He favoured negative liberty as a political ideal precisely because it does not presume to know what is good for you.

Critics pushed back. Charles Taylor, in *What's Wrong with Negative Liberty* (1979), argued that negative liberty is an **opportunity concept** (it is about the options available to you) while positive liberty is an **exercise concept** (it is about actually directing your life well). Taylor argued we cannot avoid judging that some freedoms matter more than others: the freedom to worship matters more than the freedom to drive without traffic lights. And once we make such judgments, we are already using standards about what is significant in a human life. Pure negative liberty is less innocent than it looks.

sections.heading: One Concept After All? MacCallum's Formula
sections.body:
In 1967 the American philosopher **Gerald MacCallum** argued that Berlin's two concepts were really one. Every complete statement about freedom, he said, has a **triadic** structure:

> X is (or is not) free from Y to do or become Z.

Here X is an agent, Y is some preventing condition, and Z is an action or state of being. Disputes about freedom, MacCallum argued, are really disputes about what to count as X, Y and Z.

Let's work through examples.

1. *A journalist is free to publish.* X = the journalist; Y = government censorship; Z = publishing an article. A classic negative-liberty claim.
2. *A gambler is not free to stop.* X = the gambler, conceived as his reflective self; Y = his compulsion; Z = walking away from the table. A positive-liberty claim, which treats an internal condition as a constraint.
3. *A poor family is not free to see a doctor.* X = the family; Y = lack of money; Z = receiving medical care. Whether this is a genuine unfreedom depends on whether poverty counts as a 'preventing condition' or merely as a lack of ability.

The formula clarifies arguments without settling them. Libertarians tend to count only deliberate human interference as Y. Socialists and many liberals count social structures and poverty. Positive-liberty theorists count internal obstacles like ignorance or compulsion. When two people argue about whether a policy 'increases freedom', MacCallum's advice is to fill in the triad and see where the real disagreement lies.

sections.heading: Republican Freedom: Non-Domination
sections.body:
Back to the gentle master. Neither of Berlin's concepts handles the case perfectly. The slave is interfered with little (so negatively fairly free), and might be rational and self-governing in her own thoughts (so positively free in some sense). Yet she is clearly unfree.

In the 1990s the Irish philosopher **Philip Pettit** (*Republicanism*, 1997) and the Cambridge historian **Quentin Skinner** (*Liberty before Liberalism*, 1998) revived a third concept that, they argued, had dominated Western political thought from Roman law through the English and American revolutions before being eclipsed by Hobbes and Bentham. They called it **republican** or **neo-Roman** freedom.

On this view, freedom is **non-domination**. You are dominated when another agent has the capacity to interfere in your choices **arbitrarily**, that is, at their will and pleasure, without being forced to track your interests or answer to you. Notice the key word: *capacity*. The slave is dominated even if her master never interferes, because he *could*. She must watch his moods, flatter him, keep her head down. Domination produces servility and self-censorship even without a single blow.

Conversely, you can be interfered with without being dominated. A law passed by a democratic legislature, constrained by a constitution and courts, and open to contest, interferes with you, but not arbitrarily, because it is controlled by you along with your fellow citizens. Pettit's example: a person who asks a friend to hide the cigarettes is interfered with, but on terms she controls.

Pettit offers a vivid standard, the **eyeball test**: people are free when they can look one another in the eye without reason for fear or deference that a power of interference might inspire. Republican freedom thus has implications for workplaces, marriages and bureaucracies, wherever one party holds unchecked power over another.

sections.heading: Do Markets Make Us Free?
sections.body:
These concepts become heated when applied to the economy.

**Friedrich Hayek** (1899–1992), in *The Constitution of Liberty* (1960), defined freedom as the absence of **coercion** by others, and argued that market societies maximise it. In a market, no one is forced to buy from or work for a particular person; there are always alternatives. Central planning, by contrast, concentrates power and requires officials to direct people's lives. Milton Friedman, in *Capitalism and Freedom* (1962), added that economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom, since a free press and dissent need independent sources of income.

Critics answer from each concept of freedom.

From negative liberty, **G. A. Cohen** (1941–2009) argued in an essay called *Freedom and Money* that poverty *is* a lack of negative freedom, not just of ability. Try boarding a train without a ticket: you will be physically removed. Try taking food from a shop without paying: the state will stop you. Money works like a ticket that removes these interferences. So to lack money is to be liable to interference in countless ways, and redistribution can increase negative liberty, not merely trade it away for equality.

From republicanism, **Elizabeth Anderson** in *Private Government* (2017) argued that many workers are dominated by employers who can regulate their speech, dress, bathroom breaks and even off-duty conduct, and fire them at will. The free-market ideal of independent producers trading as equals, she argues, described an eighteenth-century world of farmers and artisans; it does not describe a large modern firm. Defenders of markets reply that workers can quit, and that competition between employers limits arbitrary power. Republicans answer that exit is a weak protection when switching jobs is costly, and propose voice instead: unions, worker representation, legal protections.

The disagreement is not merely about facts. It turns on which conception of freedom you accept.

sections.heading: Taking Stock
sections.body:
Here is a compact map of the positions.

- **Negative liberty**: freedom is non-interference. Its strength is clarity and modesty: it does not tell you how to live. Its weakness: it may count the gentle master's slave as free, and it struggles to say which freedoms matter most.
- **Positive liberty**: freedom is self-mastery or effective self-government. Its strength: it captures the idea that freedom is about living by your own lights, and that a society can enable or disable this. Its weakness: Berlin's danger of 'forcing people to be free'.
- **Republican liberty**: freedom is non-domination, the secure status of not living at another's mercy. Its strength: it explains the slave case and links personal freedom to democratic institutions and checks on power. Its weakness: critics like Matthew Kramer and Ian Carter argue it can be absorbed into a sophisticated negative view (dominated people face a higher *probability* of interference), and that 'arbitrary' is hard to define.

Notice that each conception generates a different political agenda. Negative-liberty theorists focus on limiting the state. Positive-liberty theorists focus on education, health and capability, the conditions for self-direction (a theme you will meet in Lesson 5 with Nussbaum). Republicans focus on the distribution of *power*: constitutional checks, contestability, the rights of employees, tenants, spouses and citizens to answer back.

In practice, thoughtful people use all three. You can value a free press because censorship is interference, value schooling because it builds self-mastery, and value employment protections because no one should depend on a boss's goodwill.

modernConnection.title: The Algorithm as Master: Domination in the Gig Economy
modernConnection.body:
Consider a delivery rider working through an app. No manager shouts at him. He chooses when to log in. By the measure of negative liberty, he looks unusually free: there is no clock to punch, no one interfering with his day.

Now look through Pettit's lens. The app can change his pay rates overnight. It can lower his visibility to customers, or deactivate his account, often without a human explanation or a real appeal. He may not know what metrics he is judged by. Riders and drivers report adjusting their behaviour constantly to an opaque system: accepting jobs they would rather decline, avoiding complaints at any cost. That is exactly the self-censorship and anxious anticipation that republicans call domination, here exercised by software and a distant corporation rather than by a visible master.

This is why debates about **algorithmic management** have become debates about freedom. Policy responses, such as the European Union's directive on platform work adopted in 2024, focus on transparency about automated decisions, rights to human review and limits on unaccountable deactivation. In republican terms, these measures do not necessarily reduce interference; they make it *non-arbitrary*, forcing it to track rules that workers can know and contest.

The analogy has limits. A rider can switch apps or quit, which a Roman slave could not, and many value the flexibility deeply. Defenders of the platform model argue that regulation may reduce the very flexibility workers prize. That disagreement is precisely the market-freedom debate from this lesson: does exit protect freedom enough, or do people also need voice?

vocabulary.definition: Freedom understood as the absence of interference by other people.
vocabulary.example: A law banning a newspaper reduces its editors' negative liberty.

vocabulary.definition: Freedom understood as self-mastery: being governed by one's own reason and will rather than by external forces or compulsions.
vocabulary.example: An addict who regains control of his life has gained positive liberty, even if no one was interfering with him before.

vocabulary.definition: Berlin's view that genuine human values are many, can conflict, and cannot all be reconciled in one perfect arrangement.
vocabulary.example: Because of value pluralism, a society may have to choose between more security and more privacy.

vocabulary.definition: MacCallum's analysis: an agent X is free from a constraint Y to do or become Z.
vocabulary.example: Using the triadic concept of freedom, we can ask whether poverty counts as a constraint Y.

vocabulary.definition: Being subject to another agent's capacity to interfere in your choices arbitrarily, whether or not they actually do.
vocabulary.example: A tenant whose landlord can evict her at whim lives under domination even if the landlord is friendly.

vocabulary.definition: The republican ideal of freedom as secure independence from any arbitrary power.
vocabulary.example: Tenant protections promote non-domination by making eviction subject to fair rules.

vocabulary.definition: Pettit's criterion that people are free when they can look each other in the eye without fear or deference.
vocabulary.example: Workers who dare not speak up in meetings fail Pettit's eyeball test.

vocabulary.definition: Forcing someone to act by threatening harm, which Hayek treats as the central enemy of freedom.
vocabulary.example: Hayek argued that market competition limits coercion because no single employer controls your options.

thinkingExercise.title: Three Lenses on One Life
thinkingExercise.prompt: Choose a relationship of power in your own life or in the news: employee and employer, tenant and landlord, student and school, citizen and state, user and platform. Analyse it through all three concepts of freedom.
steps: Describe the relationship in two or three sentences. Who can affect whose choices, and how?
Negative lens: what interferences actually occur? Fill in MacCallum's triad for one of them.
Positive lens: does the relationship help or hinder the weaker party's capacity to direct their own life?

Republican lens: could the stronger party interfere arbitrarily? Would the weaker party pass the eyeball test? What reform would make power non-arbitrary, and would it cost anything in negative liberty?

summary: Berlin distinguished negative liberty (non-interference) from positive liberty (self-mastery) and warned that positive liberty can be twisted to justify coercion.
MacCallum argued all freedom claims share one triadic form, so disputes are about what counts as agent, constraint and goal.
Pettit and Skinner revived republican freedom as non-domination: no one should hold arbitrary power over you, even if they never use it.
Hayek and Friedman tied markets to freedom from coercion; Cohen argued poverty is a lack of negative freedom, and Anderson that workplaces can be domination.
Each concept produces a different political agenda: limiting interference, enabling self-direction, or checking arbitrary power.

quiz.question: Berlin's negative liberty is best defined as:
options: Being governed by one's rational self
The absence of interference by other people
quiz.explanation: Negative liberty concerns the area in which others leave you alone.

quiz.question: Why did Berlin think positive liberty could be dangerous?
options: Claims about a person's 'true self' can justify coercing them for their own liberation
quiz.explanation: Berlin feared that identifying freedom with a rational or collective 'real self' licenses forcing people to be free.

quiz.question: In MacCallum's formula, 'A worker is not free from debt to change careers', what is Y?
quiz.explanation: Y is the preventing condition; here, debt.

quiz.question: On the republican view, a slave with a kind master who never interferes with her is nonetheless unfree.
quiz.explanation: She is dominated because her master has the capacity to interfere arbitrarily.

quiz.question: According to Pettit, which of these involves interference without domination?
options: A dictator who rarely uses his powers
A boss who can fire you on a whim
A democratically made, contestable law limiting speed on roads
A landlord who can evict at will
quiz.explanation: Interference controlled by those affected, under rules they can contest, is not arbitrary.

quiz.question: G. A. Cohen's train ticket example aims to show that:
options: Lacking money exposes you to interference, so poverty restricts negative freedom
quiz.explanation: Without money you will be physically prevented from many actions, so poverty is a lack of freedom, not just ability.

quiz.question: Charles Taylor argued that negative liberty is an exercise concept and positive liberty an opportunity concept.
quiz.explanation: It is the reverse: negative liberty concerns available opportunities; positive liberty concerns actually exercising control over one's life.

quiz.question: Elizabeth Anderson's 'private government' refers to:
options: The power employers can hold over workers' lives
quiz.explanation: Anderson argues firms can exercise largely unaccountable authority over employees, a form of domination.

quiz.question: Which thinker defined freedom primarily as the absence of coercion and argued markets maximise it?
quiz.explanation: Hayek's Constitution of Liberty defines freedom as independence from the arbitrary will of others, secured through markets and the rule of law.

quiz.question: Value pluralism holds that all genuine values can be harmonised in a perfectly designed society.
quiz.explanation: Berlin's value pluralism denies this: real values conflict and trade-offs are unavoidable.

goDeeper.body:
Is republican freedom genuinely distinct from negative freedom? This is one of the liveliest debates in contemporary political theory. **Matthew Kramer** and **Ian Carter** defend a 'pure' negative conception on which freedom is the absence of *prevention*, measured by the combinations of actions available to you. They argue that domination reduces freedom only because it makes interference more probable, and that a sophisticated negative theory can count probable future interference. Pettit replies that this misses the point: even if the probability of interference were zero (the master is reliably kind), the slave still lives *by permission*. Her options are gifts that could be withdrawn, and that **invigilation**, the need to watch and placate, is itself the unfreedom.

Skinner's historical work adds another twist. He argues that seventeenth-century English republicans like James Harrington explicitly attacked Hobbes on this point. Hobbes had claimed that a subject in Constantinople is as free as one in republican Lucca, since what matters is how much the law actually restrains you. The republicans insisted that living under a sultan's will is servitude whatever he chooses to do. On Skinner's telling, the triumph of the negative concept was a political victory, not a philosophical discovery.

Feminist theorists have found the republican idea especially useful. Mary Wollstonecraft (Day 54) argued that married women, legally dependent on husbands, lived as dependents even in loving marriages. That is a republican argument made long before the term was revived.

readings.title: Two Concepts of Liberty
readings.author: Isaiah Berlin
readings.note: Collected in Liberty (ed. Henry Hardy); one of the most widely read essays in political philosophy.

readings.title: Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government
readings.author: Philip Pettit
readings.note: Chapters 1–2 introduce non-domination and the contrast with non-interference.

readings.title: Liberty before Liberalism
readings.author: Quentin Skinner
readings.note: A short, elegant historical recovery of the neo-Roman theory of freedom.

readings.title: Private Government
readings.author: Elizabeth Anderson
readings.note: Lively lectures applying republican ideas to the modern workplace.

questions: If a powerful agent reliably never interferes, is there anything left to fear? What does Pettit's 'invigilation' add?
Does poverty make people unfree, or merely unable? Does the answer matter politically?
Can a person be dominated by a system (an algorithm, a market) rather than by an agent?
